rows.speaker: القراء السبعة
rows.claim: The seven canonical readers vocalize the dāl of al-ḥamdu with ḍamma, making al-ḥamdu a subject and li-llāhi its predicate.
rows.anchor: القراء السبعة على ضم الدال من قوله : { الحمد لله } وهو مبتدأ وخبر .

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj read al-ḥamda with fatḥa as an implied verbal object.
rows.anchor: وروي عن سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج أنهما قالا

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Abla reads both dāl and lām with ḍamma by assimilating the second vowel to the first; Ibn Kathir calls the reading anomalous.
rows.anchor: بضم الدال واللام إتباعا للثاني الأول وله شواهد لكنه شاذ

rows.speaker: الحسن وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read the dāl with kasra by assimilating the first vowel to the second.
rows.anchor: بكسر الدال إتباعا للأول الثاني

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir explains praise as exclusive thanks to God for countless blessings, including faculties for worship, worldly provision, and guidance toward lasting bliss despite no prior entitlement.
rows.anchor: قال أبو جعفر بن جرير

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir says the phrase is God's praise of Himself and implicitly commands His servants to say it too.
rows.anchor: وفي ضمنه أمر عباده أن يثنوا عليه

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir reports a distinction that praise names God's beautiful attributes while thanks praises His favors, then argues Arabic speakers use both words interchangeably.
rows.anchor: ثناء عليه بأسمائه وصفاته الحسنى

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق وابن عطاء
rows.claim: The Sufi authorities Ja'far al-Sadiq and Ibn Ata are reported to hold that praise and thanks are equivalent.
rows.anchor: نقل السلمي هذا المذهب أنهما سواء عن جعفر الصادق وابن عطاء من الصوفية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the expression used by every grateful person.
rows.anchor: قال : قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir questions Ibn Jarir's equation: praise is verbal commendation for necessary or bestowed qualities, while thanks applies only to bestowed qualities and may be inward, spoken, or enacted.
rows.anchor: أن الحمد هو الثناء بالقول على المحمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir resolves the scope dispute by saying praise covers more kinds of objects but is speech-only, whereas thanks uses more kinds of means but concerns bestowed qualities alone.
rows.anchor: والتحقيق أن بينهما عموما وخصوصا

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines praise as the opposite of blame, says taḥmīd is more emphatic than ḥamd, and regards ḥamd as broader than thanks.
rows.anchor: حمدت الرجل أحمده حمدا ومحمدة

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines thanks as praising a benefactor for what he bestowed and says using the preposition li- is more eloquent.
rows.anchor: هو الثناء على المحسن بما أولاكه من المعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir distinguishes praise from eulogy: eulogy can concern living or dead people and even objects, precede or follow a favor, and address necessary or bestowed qualities.
rows.anchor: وأما المدح فهو أعم من الحمد

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: When Umar asks what al-ḥamdu lillāh means after learning other formulas of glorification, Ali answers that it is a phrase God approves for Himself.
rows.anchor: فقال علي : كلمة رضيها الله لنفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-ḥamdu lillāh is a word of thanks; when a servant says it, God says that His servant has thanked Him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : الحمد لله كلمة الشكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains praise as thanks, humble submission, and acknowledgment of God's favors, guidance, and origination.
rows.anchor: هو الشكر لله والاستخذاء له ، والإقرار له بنعمه

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says al-ḥamdu lillāh is God's praise.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : الحمد لله ثناء الله

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the cloak of the Most Merciful and notes that a hadith has come with a similar meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك : الحمد لله رداء الرحمن

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that whoever says al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn has thanked God, who then increases him.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Companion al-Aswad ibn Sari asks to recite praises of his Lord, and the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise.
rows.anchor: ألا أنشدك محامد حمدت بها ربي

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says the best remembrance is lā ilāha illā Allāh and the best supplication is al-ḥamdu lillāh; al-Tirmidhi grades this report ḥasan gharīb.
rows.anchor: أفضل الذكر لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Anas reports that when a servant praises God for a blessing, the reward for that praise is better than the blessing received.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال : قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi transmits a report that praising God would be better than possessing the whole world; he explains that the enduring reward for praise exceeds transient worldly enjoyment.
rows.anchor: لأن ثواب الحمد لا يفنى

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports that angels cannot calculate the full reward for a servant's praise fitting God's majesty, so God tells them to record it as said until He rewards him.
rows.anchor: فعضلت بالملكين فلم يدريا كيف يكتبانها

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: A group holds that al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn is better than lā ilāha illā Allāh because it combines praise with monotheism.
rows.anchor: قول العبد : الحمد لله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others hold that lā ilāha illā Allāh is superior because it distinguishes faith from unbelief and is the formula people must profess; reports also call it the best remembrance.
rows.anchor: لأنها الفصل بين الإيمان والكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamdu encompasses every kind and form of praise as belonging to God, as expressed in a transmitted prayer.
rows.anchor: في الحمد لاستغراق جميع أجناس الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb means owner and disposer, and in Arabic also master or one who manages something toward its good; each meaning applies to God.
rows.anchor: والرب هو : المالك المتصرف ، ويطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified title al-Rabb is used only for God; for other possessors it must be annexed, and some say al-Rabb is the greatest name.
rows.anchor: ولا يستعمل الرب لغير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, encompassing every created being besides God; created kinds in heavens, earth, land, and sea are worlds, as is each generation.
rows.anchor: كل موجود سوى الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the worlds as all creation belonging to God: heavens, earths, their inhabitants and everything between them, known and unknown.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, and other early authorities interpret the worlds as jinn and humans; Ibn Abi Hatim's chain is said to be unreliable.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس : رب الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi supports the interpretation of the worlds as jinn and humans by citing the description of the Qur'an as a warning to the worlds.
rows.anchor: واستدل القرطبي لهذا القول بقوله

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Farra and Abu Ubayda restrict the term worlds to rational beings—humans, jinn, angels, and devils—and exclude animals.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء وأبو عبيدة : العالم

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم وأبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala define worlds as everything with a spirit that receives provision.
rows.anchor: كل ما له روح يرتزق

rows.speaker: مروان بن محمد بن مروان بن الحكم
rows.claim: Ibn Asakir reports Marwan's claim that God created seventeen thousand worlds, with the inhabitants of the heavens and earth forming one and God alone knowing the rest.
rows.anchor: في ترجمة مروان بن محمد بن مروان بن الحكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says each kind or species is a world.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : رب العالمين ، كل صنف

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliyah says humans and jinn are worlds and reports uncertainty between fourteen and eighteen thousand other angelic worlds on earth, in groups worshipping God.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir calls Abu al-Aliyah's extraordinary numerical report strange and says such a claim requires sound evidence.
rows.anchor: وهذا كلام غريب يحتاج مثله إلى دليل صحيح

rows.speaker: تبيع الحميري
rows.claim: Tubyay al-Himyari says the worlds comprise one thousand nations, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
rows.anchor: عن تبيع ، يعني الحميري ، في قوله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: A similar count of one thousand worlds, divided into six hundred sea and four hundred land worlds, is also attributed to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.
rows.anchor: وحكي مثله عن سعيد بن المسيب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Jabir tells how locusts became scarce under Umar, then attributes to the Prophet a saying that there are one thousand nations and locusts are the first to perish; Ibn Kathir says Muhammad ibn Isa is weak.
rows.anchor: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Al-Baghawi reports Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's view that God has one thousand worlds, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
rows.anchor: وحكى البغوي عن سعيد بن المسيب أنه قال

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has eighteen thousand worlds and this world is one of them.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه : لله

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says there are eighty thousand worlds.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : العوالم ثمانون ألفا

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says that no one knows the number of worlds except God.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : لا يعلم عدد العوالم

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi reports from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that God has forty thousand worlds and the inhabited east-to-west world is only one.
rows.anchor: حكى القرطبي عن أبي سعيد الخدري

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines a world as everything God created in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: العالم كل ما خلق الله في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi prefers a comprehensive meaning encompassing all worlds, citing Pharaoh's question and God's identification of the Lord of the worlds as Lord of heavens, earth, and what is between them.
rows.anchor: قال القرطبي : وهذا هو الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says ʿālam derives from ʿalāmah, a sign, because every created thing points to its Maker, Creator, and oneness; he cites a poem by Ibn al-Mu'tazz.
rows.anchor: لأنه علم دال على وجود خالقه وصانعه ووحدانيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says his discussion of al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm under the basmala already covers these names, so he does not repeat it here.
rows.anchor: تقدم الكلام عليه في البسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both Māliki, meaning Owner, and Maliki, meaning King, are authentic mutawātir readings among the seven readers; Ibn Kathir regards both as sound and excellent.
rows.anchor: وكلاهما صحيح متواتر في السبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form mulayk is also mentioned, and Nafi lengthens the kasra of the kāf as maliki.
rows.anchor: وأشبع نافع كسرة الكاف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari prefers Maliki because it is the reading of the two holy cities and matches verses that explicitly speak of God's kingship.
rows.anchor: لأنها قراءة أهل الحرمين

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: A highly anomalous reading attributed to Abu Hanifa treats malaka yawma as a past-tense verb with a subject and object.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن أبي حنيفة أنه قرأ

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihab says he was told that the Prophet, early caliphs, Muawiya, and Yazid read Māliki, and that Marwan first introduced Maliki.
rows.anchor: عن ابن شهاب : أنه بلغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir pushes back on Ibn Shihab's accusation, saying Marwan knew the correctness of the reading and Ibn Shihab may not have known it.
rows.anchor: مروان عنده علم بصحة ما قرأه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh transmits reports by several routes that the Prophet recited Māliki yawmi al-dīn.
rows.anchor: وقد روي من طرق متعددة أوردها ابن مردويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik derives from ownership, as in inheriting the earth; Malik derives from sovereignty, as in the question of who holds kingship on that Day.
rows.anchor: ومالك مأخوذ من الملك ، كما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's kingship being specified for the Day of Recompense does not deny His rule over all other times; on that Day no one claims anything or speaks without His permission.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص الملك بيوم الدين لا ينفيه عما عداه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that no one shares judgment with God on that Day as earthly rulers may; it is the resurrection and reckoning, when deeds are repaid except for those God pardons.
rows.anchor: لا يملك أحد في ذلك اليوم معه حكما

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir reports an interpretation of Mālik as God being able to establish the Day of Recompense, then proceeds to weaken it.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن جرير عن بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir sees no conflict between ownership/judgment and ability to establish the Day, but says the context more strongly supports exclusive rule; the second sense resembles God's saying Be, and it is.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه لا منافاة بين هذا القول وما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is truly King; calling another person king in worldly life is metaphorical, while claiming the title King of Kings is the most contemptible name.
rows.anchor: والمَلِك في الحقيقة هو الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Hurayrah reports the Prophet's warning that the most contemptible name before God is King of Kings, since God alone is the King.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه مرفوعا أخنع اسم عند الله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet describes God folding the earth and heavens, then asking where the kings, tyrants, and arrogant people have gone.
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earthly people may be called kings only figuratively, as the Qur'an calls Talut a king and mentions a king behind others and Israelites as kings.
rows.anchor: فأما تسمية غيره في الدنيا بملك فعلى سبيل المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn means recompense and accounting, supported by Qur'anic usages and the prophetic description of the prudent person as one who takes account of himself.
rows.anchor: والدين الجزاء والحساب ؛ كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar urges people to take account of themselves before being called to account, and prepare for the great presentation before God.
rows.anchor: كما قال عمر رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: القراء السبعة والجمهور
rows.claim: The seven readers and the majority pronounce the yāʾ in iyyāka with gemination.
rows.anchor: قرأ السبعة والجمهور بتشديد الياء

rows.speaker: عمرو بن فايد
rows.claim: Amr ibn Fayd's light yāʾ with kasra is a rejected anomalous reading because iyā means sunlight.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن فايد بتخفيفها مع الكسر

rows.speaker: بعض القراء
rows.claim: Some read ayyaka with an open hamza and geminated yāʾ, while others substitute hāʾ for hamza, as illustrated by a poetic line.
rows.anchor: بالهاء بدل الهمزة ، كما قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب والأعمش
rows.claim: All readers open the initial nūn of nastaʿīn except Yahya ibn Waththab and al-A'mash, who use kasra, a dialect of several Arab tribes.
rows.anchor: وهي لغة بني أسد وربيعة وبني تميم وقيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary language ʿibādah is rooted in humility, as in a subdued road or camel; in religious usage it combines complete love, submission, and fear.
rows.anchor: العبادة في اللغة من الذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting and repeating iyyāka marks special concern and restriction: worship is for God alone and reliance is on Him alone, the perfection of obedience.
rows.anchor: وقدم المفعول وهو { إياك }

rows.speaker: بعض السلف
rows.claim: Some early authorities call this the secret of the Fatiha, itself the secret of the Qur'an: the first clause renounces shirk and the second renounces self-power through surrender to God.
rows.anchor: قال بعض السلف : الفاتحة سر القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship and reliance recur together elsewhere in the Qur'an, including commands to worship God and trust Him.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى في غير آية من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speech shifts from speaking of God in the third person to addressing Him directly because praise brings the worshipper near and present before Him.
rows.anchor: وتحول الكلام من الغيبة إلى المواجهة بكاف الخطاب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The opening is God's praise of Himself and instruction to servants to praise Him; the Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book when able.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: الله تعالى
rows.claim: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
rows.anchor: قال : هذا بيني وبين عبدي ولعبدي ما سأل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the servant worships, fears, and hopes in God alone, and seeks His help for obedience and every affair.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك ، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says God commands His servants to devote worship sincerely to Him and seek His help for their affairs.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : { إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship precedes asking for help because worship is the intended end while seeking help is its means; sound judgment puts the more important matter first.
rows.anchor: لأن العبادة له هي المقصودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of the plural nūn is that the speaker represents the whole class of worshippers, including fellow believers, especially in congregational prayer or when leading them.
rows.anchor: بأن المراد من ذلك الإخبار عن جنس العباد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation allows a plural of honor: the servant is noble while worshipping, but should not claim collective standing outside worship because everyone depends on God.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال : يجوز أن تكون للتعظيم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A third view says we is more humble than I worship because the singular could imply that one person alone can fully worship or properly praise God.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال : ألطف في التواضع من إياك أعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Servanthood is an exalted station; God calls His Messenger His servant at the revelation, public worship, and night journey, and directs him to worship amid rejection.
rows.anchor: يشرف به العبد لانتسابه إلى جناب الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some argue that servanthood is nobler than messengerhood because worship proceeds from creation to God, while the messenger's mission proceeds from God to creation; Ibn Kathir rejects the claim and its reasoning.
rows.anchor: عن بعضهم : أن مقام العبودية أشرف من مقام الرسالة

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Sufis criticize worship motivated by reward or avoidance of punishment, and even worship as honor through religious duties, arguing that the highest worship is for God's own perfection.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الصوفية : العبادة إما لتحصيل ثواب ورد عقاب

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others rebut the Sufi criticism: worship directed to God can still seek reward and protection from punishment, as the Prophet affirms to a Bedouin asking for Paradise and refuge from Hell.
rows.anchor: وقد رد ذلك عليهم آخرون وقالوا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read al-ṣirāṭ with ṣād; other readings use sīn or zāy, the latter being a dialect of several tribes according to al-Farra.
rows.anchor: قراءة الجمهور بالصاد . وقرئ :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After praising the One being asked, the sura turns to the request, an exemplary supplication that praises the addressee before asking for needs, including believers' needs.
rows.anchor: لما تقدم الثناء على المسؤول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication can also state the supplicant's need, as Moses does, combine need with praise as Jonah does, or consist of praise that itself suffices to prompt a request.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون السؤال بالإخبار عن حال السائل واحتياجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hidāyah here means guidance and enabling success; direct transitivity can mean inspire, guide, provide, or grant, while construction with ilā means show or direct, and with li means make worthy.
rows.anchor: والهداية هاهنا : الإرشاد والتوفيق

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir says interpreters unanimously understand the straight path as a clear road without crookedness, a usage confirmed by Arabic speech and poetry.
rows.anchor: أبو جعفر بن جرير : أجمعت الأمة من أهل التأويل

rows.speaker: جرير بن عطية
rows.claim: Jarir ibn Atiyyah's verse uses the straight path for a ruler who remains upright when destinations become crooked.
rows.anchor: قول جرير بن عطية الخطفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpretations of the straight path ultimately converge on following God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: ثم اختلفت عبارات المفسرين من السلف والخلف

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet through Ali identifies the straight path as the Book of God; Ibn Kathir says the report is more plausibly a statement of Ali himself.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir regards the report identifying the straight path with God's Book as more likely transmitted from Ali himself rather than from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقد روي هذا موقوفا عن علي ، وهو أشبه

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A related report calls the Qur'an God's strong rope, wise remembrance, and straight path.
rows.anchor: وهو حبل الله المتين ، وهو الذكر الحكيم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud says the straight path is the Book of God.
rows.anchor: عن منصور ، عن أبي وائل ، عن عبد الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through al-Dahhak, says the straight path is the guiding way, God's religion without deviation.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك ، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas through Maymun ibn Mihran interprets the straight path as Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال ميمون بن مهران ، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وأصحاب النبي
rows.claim: A collective report from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, and Companions of the Prophet identifies the straight path as Islam.
rows.anchor: عن مرة الهمداني ، عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jabir says the straight path is Islam and describes it as wider than the distance between heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن محمد بن عقيل ، عن جابر

rows.speaker: ابن الحنفية
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hanafiyyah says the straight path is God's religion, the only religion He accepts from servants.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الحنفية في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam also interprets the straight path as Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In an authentic report, the Prophet likens the straight path to Islam, bordered by God's limits and forbidden doors, with the Qur'an calling from its head and God's inward admonition calling from above.
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the straight path is the truth, a broader interpretation that does not conflict with the other explanations.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : { اهدنا الصراط المستقيم } ، قال : الحق

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliyah interprets the straight path as the Prophet and his two successors after him; al-Hasan says he spoke truly and advised well.
rows.anchor: للحسن ، فقال : صدق أبو العالية ونصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says all these interpretations agree: following the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar is following truth, Islam, and the Qur'an, God's strong rope and straight path.
rows.anchor: وكل هذه الأقوال صحيحة ، وهي متلازمة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: A report from Abdullah says the straight path is the way the Messenger of God left the community upon.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله ، قال : الصراط المستقيم الذي تركنا عليه رسول الله

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir prefers understanding the request as asking God to keep the worshipper steadfast in the beliefs and acts He approved and granted to those He favored, comprising Islam, revelation, obedience, and the prophetic and rightly guided way.
rows.anchor: بن جرير ، رحمه الله : والذي هو أولى بتأويل هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A believer's repeated request for guidance is not redundant: servants always need God's help to stay firm, deepen insight, grow, and continue on guidance because they control neither benefit nor harm for themselves.
rows.anchor: فالجواب : أن لا ولولا احتياجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command for believers to believe in God and revelation does not seek an already completed state; it asks for steadfastness, continuity, and perseverance in the acts that preserve faith.
rows.anchor: فقد أمر الذين آمنوا بالإيمان

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr would recite the prayer that God not let hearts deviate after guidance silently in the third unit of the Maghrib prayer, after the Fatiha.
rows.anchor: وقد كان الصديق رضي الله عنه يقرأ بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request to be guided on the straight path means asking God to keep the worshippers on it and not turn them toward another way.
rows.anchor: فمعنى قوله تعالى : { اهدنا الصراط المستقيم }
